titre: The Anglo-Zanzibar War (1896), the Shortest Ever Fought
accroche: On August 27, 1896, five British ships bombard the Sultan of Zanzibar's palace. Thirty-eight minutes later, the war is over.
contenu_vulgarise:
At nine o'clock in the morning on August 27, 1896, five Royal Navy ships open fire on the Sultan of Zanzibar's palace, off the East African coast. By nine forty, the firing stops: the palace is in ruins, the sultan's flag is down, and the war between the United Kingdom and the Sultanate of Zanzibar is over. It remains, to this day, the shortest war ever documented.

## A Dead Sultan, an Unapproved Successor

On August 25, 1896, Sultan Hamad bin Thuwaini, favorable to the British, dies suddenly. His cousin Khalid bin Barghash, twenty-nine years old, immediately moves into the palace and proclaims himself sultan, without waiting for the British consulate's approval. A treaty signed in 1890 between Zanzibar and the United Kingdom nonetheless requires this approval for any succession: London would have preferred to see Hamoud bin Muhammed take the throne. British consul Basil Cave and General Lloyd Mathews, who commands the Zanzibari forces on behalf of the protectorate, warn Khalid. He disregards them, and gathers about two thousand eight hundred men, including seven hundred regular soldiers, to defend the palace.

Rear Admiral Harry Rawson sends him an ultimatum on August 26: lower his flag and leave the palace by nine o'clock the next morning, or face bombardment. The British Foreign Secretary, Lord Salisbury, authorizes by telegram “whatever measures you may consider necessary.” On the morning of August 27, at eight thirty, Cave has a final message delivered to Khalid: “We do not want to open fire, but unless you do as you are told we shall certainly do so.” Khalid does not respond.

## Thirty-Eight Minutes, Five Ships

At nine-oh-two, the guns of the ships Racoon, Thrush and Sparrow open fire simultaneously; the first shell from Thrush immediately disables a Zanzibari cannon. The royal yacht Glasgow attempts to fire back at nine-oh-five and is sunk at once. By around nine forty, the palace is in ruins and the flag is down: historians most often give thirty-eight minutes of bombardment, some counting up to forty-five depending on the exact moment chosen to mark the end of the fighting. The toll is one-sided: about five hundred dead and wounded on the Zanzibari side, civilians included, against a single wounded British sailor. Khalid escapes through a back door, takes refuge at the German consulate, and sails in October for German East Africa. Hamoud bin Muhammed, London's approved candidate, is installed as sultan that same afternoon, with sharply reduced powers.

## A Sovereignty That Was No Longer One

Zanzibar never declared war on the United Kingdom in the usual sense of the term: the sultanate had been a protectorate since 1890, and the new sultan installed that day ruled under direct British control. The swiftness of the outcome owes less to the firepower deployed than to the absence of any real balance of power between the two sides. A protectorate can carry the title of sultanate, fly its own flag, raise an army several thousand strong, and still remain a territory administered elsewhere. What thirty-eight minutes of cannon fire mainly demonstrated is where the real decision had already lain since 1890.

carte.punch: The shortest war in history lasted thirty-eight minutes, on August 27, 1896.
carte.idee: On August 27, 1896, five British ships bombard the Sultan of Zanzibar's palace for thirty-eight minutes, to install the sultan London had chosen. Zanzibar remained a protectorate: its displayed sovereignty carried no weight against the real control exercised since 1890.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: The official compendium of treaties concerning Africa, which includes the June 1890 agreement placing the Sultanate of Zanzibar under British protection: the very text Khalid bin Barghash disregarded by seizing the palace in 1896.

quiz.question: Why did the Anglo-Zanzibar War of 1896 end within thirty-eight minutes?
choix: Because Sultan Khalid's army, too small, scattered as soon as the first shots were fired
Because Khalid bin Barghash had agreed to give up the palace before the ultimatum
Because a peace treaty signed the day before had already set the terms of surrender
Because Zanzibar remained a British protectorate, with no real balance of power against London
quiz.explication: Zanzibar had been a protectorate since 1890: the treaty already required British approval for any succession. Khalid's army, nearly two thousand eight hundred strong, did not scatter before the shelling; no prior peace treaty existed; and Khalid refused to yield until the bombardment began.
